title: Meet the 20 new MacArthur Fellows, the ‘genius grant’ winners of 2026
text:
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Meet the 20 new MacArthur Fellows, the ‘genius grant’ winners of 2026

Among the winners of 2026 MacArthur Fellowships is Vincenzo Vitelli, a 48-year-old theoretical physicist at the University of Chicago.

On Tuesday morning, as has been happening annually since 1981, a small number of people have had their lives changed. This year, there are 20 of them, a group that has been formally announced as recipients of the 2026 MacArthur Fellowships, those so-called “genius grants.”

Spread across the globe, these people will be receiving monetary awards of $800,000, paid out in annual installments of $160,000 over five years. Candidates are nominated by outside sources. “Nominees are suggested by a constantly changing pool of invited external nominators,” according to the Chicago-based MacArthur Foundation, “chosen from as broad a range of fields and areas of interest as possible.”

The foundation further informs us that a “fellowship is not a reward for past accomplishment, but rather an investment in a person’s originality, insight and potential.” Naturally, the foundation hopes that its money will be used by recipients for the financial freedom that might allow them to pursue their most innovative ideas and, in so doing, enrich the planet.

Vincenzo Vitelli is a 48-year-old theoretical physicist at the University of Chicago. According to the MacArthur Foundation, “his work has led to major advances in diverse fields such as metamaterials, information physics, liquid crystals, spin glasses, and the modeling of complex systems — both biological and non-biological, and far from equilibrium.”

That’s a bit above my head, and I told Vitelli so when we connected via Zoom on Sunday from Paris, where he is spending a few months at the CNRS (Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique), France’s state-funded public research organization and the largest fundamental research agency in Europe.

He is with his wife, Leontine van Cleef, and their first child, the 5-month old Felix who was born in Chicago. In conversation, he was warm and friendly, talking about his affection for Chicago, Paris and Italy.

He is naturally delighted by honor, though when first informed by telephone “I thought it was a prank, a joke. Of course it is very exciting for me and for my family, though it will be some years before Felix is able to understand.”

Vitelli was raised in the ancient southern Italian city of Matera, the son of Franco Vitelli, a literary critic, and mother Caterina, was a school teacher who wrote for the local newspapers.

His father often took business trips to Milan, and always returned from those trips with books for Vincenzo. “Most of them were books for children,” he told me. “They gave me my first exposure to the outside world and one of them really introduced me to what would become my academic passion. It was called ‘The Great Book of Science.”

In high school, he loved math and, during a summer in England, learned English. He obtained a bachelor’s degree in theoretical physics from Imperial College London in 2000 and a doctorate in physics from Harvard University in 2006.

He was a professor in the Institute Lorentz for theoretical physics in Leiden University in the Netherlands, which is where he met his wife. He came here in 2017 to become a professor at the University of Chicago. Van Cleef earned a master’s degree in architecture, specializing in interior architecture, at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago.

The family will return to Chicago in December and settle back into their South Loop home. He has yet to make plans for the MacArthur money but he does say that “there are some ideas I would like to pursue and I am sure we will use some of it on Felix.”

The other members of the 2026 class of MacArthur Fellows, in alphabetical order, as announced by the MacArthur Foundation:

Holly Jean Buck, University of Buffalo in New York (45): Sociologist investigating the social, ethical and political dimensions of climate and energy policies and emerging technologies.
